archetype.name: Game Manager (reined-in)
archetype.definition: A second-year former No. 1 pick being asked to protect the ball inside a run-leaning plan, living underneath and short of the sticks while the vertical part of his game has gone missing.

report.headline: Safer, shorter, and still sinking: the leash is costing Ward his best throws.
report.take:
Cam Ward's second season looks like a coaching staff's answer to a rookie year that ranked 51st of 63 in EPA per play. Robert Saleh's Titans pass far less than situation predicts (-8.5 pass rate over expected, 30th), and Ward has been pulled in. His aggressiveness fell from 12.6% to 8.47%, his intended air yards sit at 6.78, and his average throw lands 2.66 yards short of the sticks. The cleanup worked on the surface. His bad-throw rate dropped 4.6 points, his CPOE improved by 1.5, and his pressure-to-sack rate fell from 32.2% last year to 22.7%. The protection in front of him is also among the league's best at keeping him clean (3rd in hit rate allowed).

None of that has turned into offense. He is 38th of 45 in EPA per dropback at -0.182, 40th in yards per attempt, and the unit is 31st overall. The damage comes from two ends of the field. Throws behind the line cost the offense 11 points of EPA, which reflects a screen game that isn't working, not wild decisions. His 15 deep attempts produced a 13.3% completion rate, -0.889 EPA per throw and an interception. The one zone that works is the one the plan uses least: on 40 intermediate throws he's at +0.157 EPA per play. The short game is accurate (+3.8 CPOE) but barely breaks even, so a lot of completions are buying very little.

The ugliest splits point to structure as much as to Ward. Third downs come at 8.9 yards to go on average, and he converts 27.5% of them. Under center he has thrown 3 interceptions on 26 attempts at -0.462 EPA, which is where the run-heavy play-action looks are failing. Throws over the middle (-0.522 EPA, 2 picks) show he still struggles to read and fit the ball between the hashes. He has also been worse in one-score games (-0.289) than when trailing by two scores, so garbage time is not inflating these numbers. If anything, it is propping them up. His fantasy floor rests on legs and goal-line luck: designed runs at +0.676 EPA and two rushing touchdowns in Week 2.

Week 4 at Baltimore showed the version that can work: 222 yards, positive EPA, +6.8 CPOE and a 7.7% bad-throw rate. Houston then pressured him on 36.6% of dropbacks and he collapsed to -16.9 EPA. A win at Indianapolis came despite an 11-of-22, 102-yard day. Over his last three games his CPOE is -5.2 and his interception rate is up 1.1 points. The conservative version isn't stabilizing; it's sliding back toward last year with less upside.

strengths.title: Intermediate window actually produces
strengths.body: On throws of 10 to 19 air yards he's the positive-EPA passer the Titans drafted. The completion rate is modest, but the gains are big enough to pay for the misses. It's the clearest argument for loosening the leash, since it is the one depth where his arm and timing beat the defense.

strengths.title: Cleaner mechanics, fewer drive-killing sacks
strengths.body: His bad-throw rate and pressure-to-sack rate both improved sharply on last season. Behind a line that ranks 3rd in hits allowed, his sack rate is below league average. This looks like real development in pocket handling rather than noise, because it shows up across most games.

strengths.title: Legs as a quiet efficiency source
strengths.body: His designed runs and scrambles are both positive-EPA plays, and four of the 12 scrambles moved the chains. The volume is small, and the two rushing touchdowns came in one game, but the running is a genuine add in an offense that needs any positive play it can find.

concerns.title: The deep ball has vanished
concerns.body: Fifteen deep attempts have produced a 13.3% completion rate, a -24.9 CPOE and -13.3 total EPA, the single biggest drain on his line. Fifteen throws is a small sample, and some of this is the plan throwing deep rarely and predictably. Still, last year's profile was also inaccurate, so a full bounce-back shouldn't be assumed.

concerns.title: Conservatism without payoff
concerns.body: Throwing short of the sticks with low aggressiveness has made him more accurate but not more efficient. Screens and throws behind the line are deep in the red, and third downs arrive long and mostly fail. That's partly scheme and partly Ward declining the tight-window throws a starter has to make.

concerns.title: Middle of the field and under center
concerns.body: Throws over the middle and dropbacks from under center are where his interceptions cluster. Both samples are small, but they point to the same thing: reading leverage on in-breaking routes after a play fake is not there yet. In one-score games, the moments that decide outcomes, his efficiency is at its worst.

trend.note: Weeks 2 and 4 were near break-even and showed real accuracy. Since then, Houston's pressure produced his worst game, and Indianapolis held him to 102 yards on a -20.1 CPOE despite the win. His last three games trail his season in CPOE and interception rate.

nextGame.headline: Cleveland's thinned interior opens a window against a top-ten pass defense
nextGame.body:
Cleveland is a top-10 pass defense with a rush that ranks 5th in hit rate and 4th in sack rate, exactly the pressure that broke Ward against Houston. The tight-end lane is shut (2nd-stingiest EPA allowed to TE1s), which hurts given Gunnar Helm is already a negative-EPA target. The softer spots are the WR2 role, where Cleveland is 28th in EPA allowed, and explosive runs, where it is last. Expect the Titans to lean on the ground game and keep Ward on schedule in a game the Book sees as a coin flip with a 38.5 total. That is also another one-score script, his weakest state.

Availability tilts things somewhat his way. Cleveland's defensive tackles Mason Graham and Mike Hall Jr. were listed out as of Oct. 19, and Kalia Davis is on IR. That strips much of the interior push, the pressure that most disrupts a 2.9-second time to throw. Safety Grant Delpit is questionable with a concussion, and losing him would loosen the intermediate middle where Ward has to improve. Tennessee lists no offensive injuries, so his full protection and receiver group should be intact.

keyMatchups.title: Titans line vs. depleted interior
keyMatchups.body: Cleveland's pressure numbers are top five, but three interior linemen are out or on IR. If the edges can't win alone, Ward gets the clean pockets he had in Weeks 2 and 4. If they can, it looks like the Houston game.

keyMatchups.title: Robinson in the WR2 soft spot
keyMatchups.body: Cleveland has been generous to second receivers by EPA, and Wan'Dale Robinson fills that role behind Carnell Tate. Tate is the only target producing clearly positive EPA for Ward, so getting both going is how this passing game clears 200 yards.

keyMatchups.title: Run game sets the script
keyMatchups.body: Cleveland allows explosive runs at the league's worst rate, and Tennessee already runs well above expectation. A working ground game means fewer Ward dropbacks but shorter third downs, the situation he badly needs.

nextGame.watch: Whether he takes intermediate shots between the numbers with Delpit possibly out, or keeps checking down short of the sticks.

restOfSeason.body:
The volume is what it is: a run-leaning team, fewer than 30 attempts a game and a 1-5 record that hasn't forced the Titans to throw more. The improved accuracy underneath and lower sack rate look real and should keep the floor from collapsing. The deep-ball numbers are bad enough on 15 throws that some regression upward is likely, simply because a 13.3% completion rate is hard to sustain. The rushing touchdowns, though, came in one game and shouldn't be counted on. Expect roughly 160 to 200 passing yards a week and something like one touchdown pass a game at best, with interceptions staying near his current rate while he fights the middle of the field.

The bigger question is whether the staff widens the plan. His intermediate efficiency and his best game at Baltimore both came when he pushed the ball more. If aggressiveness creeps back toward last year's level, the yardage ceiling rises, but so does the interception risk.
swingFactors: Staff loosening the leash on intermediate and deep throws

confidence.note: Six starts with a consistent role; efficiency matches last year's weak profile, though depth splits are small.
